_areas_note: One peak, one trailhead: Goat Mountain trail 673, leaving the Hannegan Pass road (FS 32) about 2.3 miles up from the Mount Baker Highway east of Glacier, at roughly 2,500 ft on the north side of the Ruth Creek valley. VERIFIED AS BELONGING HERE. The south ridge scramble is the only standard way up the mountain and it starts on this trail; there is no other road, spur or path that serves it. The trail switchbacks hard out of the forest for about two and a half miles, enters the Mount Baker Wilderness roughly two miles up, and the maintained tread ends around 5,400 ft on the mountain's shoulder, after which a steep boot path climbs open grass and heather to the west summit and the crest continues east over rougher ground to the higher east peak. NOT DUPLICATED FROM THE HANNEGAN AND NOOKSACK ZONE: that file's camps are further up the same road at the Ruth Creek road end and the Nooksack Cirque spur, on the far, south side of the valley, and serve Ruth, Icy, Sefrit and Nooksack Tower. Goat Mountain is the north wall of the same valley and shares none of that ground. THE WATER SITUATION IS THE DEFINING FACT OF THIS ZONE and it is not shared by its neighbours. Streams cross the trail repeatedly through the forest, but the last of them is at roughly mile 2.7, right where the tread breaks into the meadows. Everything above that — the benches, the 5,200 ft knob, the ridge crest to 5,600 ft and beyond — is a dry, south-facing crest with no reliable water at all. A party that camps high without filling up in the forest has no options short of descending. The one exception is the basin under the east peak, which holds both flat ground and water. Because the slope faces south it melts out early and the season runs long, which is exactly why it dries out.

sites.name: Last stream crossing, top of the forest
sites.capacity: One or two tents on rough ground beside the trail where the timber gives out; there is no established site and the slope is steep, so flat spots are few
sites.water: THIS IS THE LAST RELIABLE WATER ON THE MOUNTAIN, at roughly mile 2.7 where the final creeks cross the tread. Treat it. Everything on the ridge above is dry, so fill every container here whether or not you intend to camp
sites.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, inside the Mount Baker Wilderness, whose boundary the trail crosses around mile 2. No overnight permit is required and none is issued. Twelve-person party limit. Campfires are not permitted on this trail, so carry a stove. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required at the trailhead; a Washington Discover Pass is not valid here. Black bears work this slope in huckleberry season and food must be secured overnight
sites.notes: Listed for the water rather than for the camping, and the water is the point. The trail climbs steeply from the trailhead through about a dozen switchbacks in the first mile and stays in deep forest for two and a half, crossing several small creeks on the way; the highest of them sits right where the trees thin into heather and huckleberry. Above this line the mountain gives you nothing. Parties heading to the benches or the crest should stop here, top up, and accept carrying the weight for the last stretch. Late in a dry summer even these crossings run thin, so do not assume the lower ones are still flowing on the way down. Elevation is not stated because the exact crossing shifts with the season and the snowpack; navigate to it by the transition out of the timber, not by an altimeter reading.

sites.name: Open benches on the broad ridge
sites.capacity: Two or three small tents spread across the benches, kept apart so the heather is not trampled into one bare patch
sites.water: NONE. Everything must be carried up from the last crossing in the forest. Snow patches linger into July in shaded pockets and can be melted early in the season, but by August the whole crest is dry
sites.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit required, twelve-person party limit, recreation pass at the trailhead. No campfires. Camp on bare ground, gravel or an existing flat rather than in the heather, and store food securely against bears
sites.notes: The best camping on the mountain if you are willing to haul water, and the natural base for the south ridge scramble. A series of level shelves on a broad, open ridge above treeline, past a viewpoint knob near 5,200 ft, with Baker, Shuksan and Sefrit filling the skyline and the Border Peaks and the Pickets beyond. From here the maintained trail continues to its end on the shoulder and the scramble to the summits goes on from there, so a camp at the benches leaves a short and pleasant summit morning. The slope faces south and melts early, so this is usually accessible from late June, sometimes earlier; the trade is that it bakes and stays dry all summer. It is fully exposed to wind and to weather rolling in from the west with nothing to duck behind. Excellent huckleberries in early autumn, and bears know it.

sites.name: Ridge crest at the end of the maintained trail
sites.capacity: One or two tents on the shoulder where the tread runs out; small, stony and windy
sites.water: NONE, and the nearest is the forest crossings far below. In early season there are snow patches on the north side of the crest to melt; from midsummer there is nothing at all
sites.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit, twelve-person limit, recreation pass at the trailhead, no campfires. This is national forest rather than national park — the park boundary lies well east beyond Hannegan Pass — so no park backcountry permit applies
sites.notes: The highest ground with anything like a flat pitch, where the maintained trail ends on Goat Mountain's shoulder and the route becomes a steep boot path up grass and heather to the false summit and the west peak. The crest carries on upward from here toward 5,600 ft and above, and the east peak, which is the higher of the two, is a further meadow scramble along the ridge with no trail. Camping here shortens summit day to almost nothing, which is the only argument for it: it is stony, cramped and completely exposed, and it is the driest spot on a dry mountain. Snow can lie across the upper slope into July and the grass traverse above is genuinely slippery when wet, so this is a fair-weather choice. Sunrise and sunset from the crest are the reason people put up with all of it.

sites.name: Basin below the east peak
sites.capacity: Two or three tents with room to spread out; the most generous ground on the mountain
sites.water: Present, which makes this basin unique here — snowmelt streams and pools that last well into the season, unlike anything on the crest. Treat it, and check that it is still running before relying on it in a dry late summer
sites.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit required, twelve-person party limit, recreation pass at the trailhead, no campfires. Camp on durable ground away from the water and secure food overnight
sites.notes: The one camp on Goat Mountain that solves the water problem, in the basin lying east and below the higher east peak, seen from the overlook near the top of the maintained trail. It has ample flat terrain and running water, which nothing on the ridge does. The cost is that reaching it means leaving the trail entirely and dropping off the crest on trackless ground, which is more commitment than most parties want for a scramble that can be done in a day from the benches — so it is chosen mainly by people camping two nights, going for the east summit as well as the west, or arriving too late in the season for the crest to hold snow. Approach it from the end of the maintained trail rather than trying to contour in low. No elevation is given because the usable ground spreads across the basin floor rather than sitting at one identifiable spot.
